title: First Passage in the Presence of Jump Rate Fluctuations: A Transition from Infinite to Finite Mean
abstract: A simple symmetric random walk on a one-dimensional lattice is guaranteed to reach any target site, yet its mean first-passage time diverges. Here, we show that stochastic fluctuations in the jump rate can fundamentally alter this classic result. We find a phase transition in the mean first-passage time: sufficiently broad rate fluctuations render it finite, whereas weaker fluctuations leave it infinite. Our results demonstrate that temporal fluctuations in the jump rate---and hence in the diffusivity---can overcome spatial wandering and regularize otherwise divergent first-passage times.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes a random walk whose jump rate fluctuates stochastically. It discovers a critical transition point: if the rate fluctuations are strong enough, the mean time to reach a target site becomes finite, overcoming the natural divergence seen in simple random walks. This demonstrates that temporal noise can fundamentally regularize spatial transport dynamics.
main_problem: The paper investigates how stochastic fluctuations in the jump rate of a random walk fundamentally alter its mean first-passage time (MFPT), potentially causing a transition from an infinite to a finite mean.
main_result: A phase transition occurs at a critical fluctuation parameter ($\alpha_c = 1/2$): when fluctuations are sufficiently broad ($\alpha < 1/2$), the MFPT becomes finite, whereas weaker fluctuations ($\alpha \ge 1/2$) leave it infinite.
method: The analysis uses the framework of the Doubly Stochastic Continuous-Time Random Walk (DSCTRW), employing Laplace transforms and asymptotic analysis of the survival probability $S(t|x_0)$.
model_or_system: The model is a simple symmetric random walk on a 1D lattice, generalized to a DSCTRW where the jump rate ($\lambda_t$) itself is a stochastic process, specifically resampled from a Mittag-Leffler distribution.
key_observables: Mean First Passage Time (MFPT) and the Survival Probability $S(t|x_0)$.
important_parameters: The Mittag-Leffler distribution parameter $\alpha$, which dictates the rate fluctuation strength; the critical value $\alpha_c = 1/2$.
main_assumptions: The jump rate is assumed to be resampled every fixed time interval $	au_r$, and the analysis relies on asymptotic power-law decay of the survival probability.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the DSCTRW process, the asymptotic power-law decay of the survival probability $S(t|x_0) \propto t^{-1/2\alpha}$, and the phase transition of the MFPT versus the fluctuation parameter $\alpha$ and relaxation time $	au_r$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the mathematical machinery for the DSCTRW, derives the asymptotic decay of the survival probability using Laplace transforms, and then analyzes the resulting MFPT to pinpoint the critical transition point governed by the rate fluctuation parameter $\alpha$.
why_interesting: The concept of temporal fluctuations regularizing otherwise divergent spatial transport times is highly relevant to open quantum systems, anomalous diffusion in disordered media, and quantum transport where noise sources are inherent.

In this particular example, the jump rate is resampled, from an exponential distribution with unit mean, at fixed time intervals of length τr = 5 [a.u.].

FIG. 2. DSCTRW Recipe. Follow these steps to obtain the probability to be at position⃗r at time t in the DSCTRW. Step 1: Start with the probability to be at⃗r after n steps for the discrete-time random walk. Step 2: Convert steps to time: Multiply the probability in step 1 by χn(t), the probability to take n steps by time t given a specific realization of the cumulative jump rate Λt. This is a Poisson distribution with mean Λt. Then, sum over all steps. Step 3: Average over all possible cumulative rates Λt.

Fig. 4(b) exhibits rich behavior of the MFPT. First, as α  0, the MFPT converges to τr regardless of its value. This is not a coincidence. In this limit, the Mittag-Leffler distribution becomes increasingly concentrated at two extremes: rate zero and rate infinity. The probability of sampling either converges to half. Thus, sampling a rate is analogous to flipping a coin: heads for rate zero; tails for rate infinity. When we flip tails (rate infinity), the walker reaches the target in zero time. This occurs on average after two flips. As we first flip at t = 0, and then again every τr, the second flip is at t = τr. Therefore, the MFPT is τr.
